sentences.text: Nadia's grandfather lived in a small village of mud-brick houses at the very edge of the dunes.
His name was Sidi Hassan, but everyone called him just Sidi.
He was seventy-one, and he was thin, and he had the kind of dark weathered skin that comes from spending a life in the sun, and he did not talk very much.
His village was called Merzouga, and it was in the southeastern part of Morocco, in a region where the paved road ran out and the huge orange dunes of the Erg Chebbi began.
Nadia had come to visit him for two weeks, in the winter, when the desert was not too hot.
She was twelve, and she lived the rest of the year in the city of Meknes, far to the north.
She had visited Sidi many times as a small child, but not since she was seven.
She had almost forgotten the smell of his house — mint tea and cedar smoke and dry dust.
She had almost forgotten how the light came into the small rooms through slits in the wooden shutters.
She had almost forgotten, most of all, the silence.
Merzouga was quiet in a way that Meknes never was.
On her second morning, Sidi took Nadia to meet the camel.
His name was Farouk.
He was old — twenty-two years old, which Sidi said was very old for a working camel — and he had been Sidi's camel for eighteen of those years.
Farouk lived in a small stone corral behind Sidi's house.
He was tan and huge and had big soft eyes and a mouth that always seemed to be chewing something.
Sidi patted his neck and Farouk lowered his enormous head to be scratched between the ears.
"Farouk knows the desert better than I do," Sidi said.
He said this in the very serious way he said everything.
"He has been out there a thousand times.
If we get lost, we trust him.
That is a rule.
Do not forget it.
If we are ever in the desert and I say — trust the camel — then you do exactly what he does.
Walk where he walks.
Do not go in any other direction.
Do you understand." Nadia nodded.
She did not think she would ever be in a situation where she needed to remember this.
But she nodded.
Sidi was one of the last men in the village who still knew the old wells.

The dunes of the Erg Chebbi covered maybe fifty square kilometers, and in them, hidden and long forgotten by most people, were maybe twenty small wells — dug hundreds of years ago by nomads, kept in secret.
Sidi's father had taught him where they were, and his father before that, going back many generations.
The wells were mostly not used anymore — the village had a big new well of its own that had been drilled with modern equipment.
But Sidi still visited the old ones.
He said they were his responsibility.
"Every few weeks I go and clean one," he told Nadia.
"I take a bucket, I take a small brush, I take a piece of cloth.
I clean out the sand and I make sure the water is still good.
It is a small work but it keeps them alive.
If nobody remembers where they are, and if they fill in with sand, they are gone forever.
And someday, someday if the modern well fails, this village will need them again.
So I keep them."
"How many people know where they are," Nadia asked.
Sidi held up one hand.
Then he lowered a finger.
"Four," he said.
"Me.
My older brother in Rissani.
Two younger men in the village that I have been teaching.
That is all.
When we die — well.
We do not want them to die with us.
That is why we teach."
"Nadia," Sidi said, on the third day.
"I want to take you to one.
Tomorrow.
It is far.
Six hours by camel, out and back.
I want you to see.
Not so you can be one of the four.
That is not — that is not how it works.
But so you can know they exist.
So when you are grown up, and if the village needs to know that some old man in a book once knew where they were, you can say — yes, my grandfather knew them.
You can tell people.
Even if you do not have the map yourself."
Nadia said yes.
That evening Sidi prepared.
He filled two big goatskins of water.
He packed dates and small round pieces of dry flatbread.
He got out an old wool blanket in case they had to rest in the sun.
He checked Farouk's saddle.
He rolled up a small piece of paper that had, on it, a hand-drawn map of the dunes.
It had eleven small crosses on it.
He tapped one of them.
"That one," he said.
"That is where we go tomorrow.
Its name is Bir Amina.
The well of Amina.
Nobody knows anymore who Amina was.
But she is in the name."
They left before dawn.
It was cold — much colder than Nadia had expected.
She had put on all her layers, and Sidi had wrapped a long piece of indigo cloth around her head and over her nose, leaving only her eyes visible.
He was dressed the same.
Farouk carried the water and the food and Nadia.
Sidi walked ahead.
He said walking kept his legs strong, and that he could always ride if he needed to.
The sky slowly went pink, then orange, then a very pale blue.
They went up into the dunes.
Behind them the village grew smaller.
Ahead of them was only sand — one dune after another, each one exactly like the last, and yet each one somehow different.
